summary: EmberRadar turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS satellite fire detections into a burning activity calendar for any area of the United States. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) see fire differently: VIIRS detects about twice as much. We harmonize them into one consistent record by counting "fire-days" (25 km squares with fire each day) and calibrating VIIRS to MODIS month by month, so there is no artificial jump in 2012. The web app shows when an area usually burns, which months and years were unusual, how the current month compares with the historical median, and whether activity is trending up or down. It has three views for emergency responders, land managers and researchers. Users can select a state, draw an area, upload a boundary or enter coordinates. They can compare periods, download analytics and hotspot CSVs, and ask questions that are answered from the data on screen. This gives people who plan for fire a reliable long-term baseline: when to staff up, when the quieter windows for prescribed burning usually fall, and whether this year is unusual.
details:
What it does

EmberRadar is a web app and open API that combines NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire records into a single burning activity calendar for the United States, from November 2000 to today. For any area it shows the months that usually burn, the normal (median) for each month, unusually high or low months, yearly totals, the long-term trend, and how the current month and latest week compare with normal.

How it works

We developed a data pipeline that retrieves the complete FIRMS archive and the near-real-time data feed, and harmonizes the two sensors in four stages.

1. Data cleaning: Only vegetation fires are retained. Detections from volcanoes, gas flares and other industrial heat sources are removed so that they do not distort the analysis.

2. Fire-day aggregation: Rather than counting individual detections, which depend heavily on sensor resolution, we count "fire-days." A 25 km grid cell with at least one detection on a given day is recorded as one fire-day. This measure captures the spatial and temporal extent of burning and removes most of the difference between the 1 km resolution of MODIS and the 375 m resolution of VIIRS.

3. Cross-sensor calibration: For each calendar month, we compare VIIRS and MODIS fire-days on days when both satellites provided complete coverage (2012–2021). This yields monthly calibration factors ranging from 1.85 to 2.71, reflecting the seasonal variation in the relationship between the two sensors.

4. Record integration: The calibrated data are merged into a single daily record. Each day uses the most reliable available sensor, VIIRS observations are converted to MODIS-equivalent values using the corresponding monthly factor, and days with missing or incomplete satellite coverage are recorded as missing data rather than as an absence of fire. The result is a continuous series from 2000 to the present with no discontinuity at 2012.

Building on this harmonized record, the monthly baseline is defined as the median of previous years. Anomalous months are identified using a robust statistical measure that is not distorted by single extreme years, and long-term trends are assessed with the Mann-Kendall test and Sen's slope estimator, both established methods in climate and environmental research. All calibration factors and parameters are published through an open API, allowing the methodology to be independently verified.

Benefits and intended impact

The challenge identifies three user groups, and the application opens with the question most relevant to each.

- Emergency management and fire response: whether current activity is above normal and where the largest fires are located. Results use the same "above, near or below normal" terminology as national fire outlooks, and a printable briefing is provided.

- Land management: when the fire season occurs, when activity is historically lower, and whether patterns are changing. This supports the planning of prescribed burns and seasonal resource allocation.

- Research: whether observed trends are statistically meaningful and how the sensor records were combined. The application presents raw and harmonized data side by side, the results of the trend analysis, and an independent check of whether MODIS alone confirms each anomalous month.

Users can download monthly analytics and hotspot data in CSV format for any date range, generate printable reports and share direct links to any view. An optional assistant answers free-text questions about the selected area using only the figures displayed in the application, ensuring that responses remain grounded in the data and never constitute forecasts.

Our intended impact is a reliable long-term baseline for fire activity. As the MODIS satellites approach the end of their missions, a calibrated bridge between the two sensors preserves the value of 26 years of fire history alongside the VIIRS record.

Tools and technologies

The data pipeline is written in Python. The API is written in TypeScript and deployed on Cloudflare Workers, using a D1 database for the harmonized daily and monthly records and R2 storage for the raw hotspot data. The front end is built with JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Mapbox GL JS for 3D mapping. The optional assistant uses Cloudflare Workers AI (Llama 3.3 70B) and is restricted to the figures presented in the application.

Creativity and design considerations

Many fire-monitoring tools present data from a single sensor or display both sensors without reconciling them. Our approach establishes comparability between the sensors first, and then designs the interface around the questions each user group needs answered. The application adopts formats already familiar to practitioners, including the terminology of national fire outlooks, the "current year versus normal" presentation used in firefighter pocket cards, and colour-blind-safe colour scales.

Transparency about uncertainty was a central design principle. The application identifies areas where limited data reduce confidence, distinguishes provisional near-real-time data, separates missing observations from the absence of fire, and states clearly that historical patterns do not constitute a forecast. Because satellites cannot distinguish wildfires from planned burns, the calendar represents all burning activity, and fire-days describe the extent of burning rather than the size of individual fires.
